---
title: "Caveats and Performance"
guide-section: "Reference"
---

What to know before relying on tether in a pipeline: the limits of the
model, the limits of each backend, and what the commands cost.

## Limits of the model

### No cross-system atomicity

A commit records each object's state within a capture window;
point-consistency requires quiesced writers. The Neon quiescence check
helps ([Neon](#neon)), but nothing coordinates two systems. `promote` lands
system by system, and a failure part-way leaves the earlier ones landed
([Landing it](04-branching-and-writing.qmd#landing-it-tether-promote)).
Promotion is per system too: a system with no merge refuses a diverged base.

### Concurrent writers on one branch

Two writers on one store branch (a `--shared` bookmark, two clones on one
bookmark) are ordered by a compare-and-swap only where the backend has one:
git, and Icechunk on `s3://`. Icechunk on local storage and Lance check the
head just before moving it, which leaves a window
([conditional moves](07-cli.qmd#conditional-moves)). Keep such writers on
one checkout, or give each its own bookmark.

### Native handles do not follow `new`

Every `open` follows the bookmark the checkout is on now, but a handle
already open keeps writing to the branch it was opened on. A notebook that
opened a handle before another process ran `tether new -b` writes to the
old branch. Open the object again after a `new`.

### Icechunk never reuses a deleted tag name

A `tether.*` tag deleted by hand, or released by a `gc` you then regret,
cannot be recreated under its name: Icechunk keeps a tombstone. tether
keeps the pin id and moves the *ref* on instead. `repair`, or the next
commit of that state, creates `tether.<id>.2`, then `.3`, and readers
resolve a pin through its live generation. So nothing is lost while the
store keeps the snapshot. There are a thousand generations per id.

### Pin-then-commit ordering

Pins are created before the VCS commit. If anything after them fails (a
manifest write, a listing, the VCS commit), `commit` releases the pins it
created and puts the manifests back. It never releases a pin an earlier
commit made and this one reused. If the process dies outright, its journal
entry stays `INCOMPLETE`, and `gc` from any checkout keeps the pins that
entry names; re-running the commit finishes it. One thing is never undone:
a dataset commit that landed. If the adapter fails *after* writing it,
history already names the pins, so the commit stands and the error is
reported. Re-run `tether verify` after merging manifests across branches.

### One writer per checkout, one per repository

Every writing command takes an advisory lock on the checkout
(`.tether/lock`). `commit`, `pull`, `new`, `restore`, `gc`, `drop`,
`abandon`, `undo` and `repair`, and any lazy fork a writable `open`
performs, also take `tether.lock` in the VCS's shared directory, which
every checkout of the repository shares. So a `gc` here cannot race a
commit in another workspace, and two checkouts cannot both find a branch
absent and fork over each other. A second command waits, then gives up
with a message naming the lock (30 s for the checkout, 60 s for the
repository). Threads sharing one `Repo` take turns the same way. Separate
clones share no lock.

### Windows

Windows has no `fcntl`, so nothing can order two processes. Commands that
write are refused there with one message, and a default `open` is
read-only. `status`, `verify`, `diff`, `log`, `ops` and `gc --dry-run`
work. Run the writing commands from a POSIX system, or WSL, until the lock
has a Windows implementation. Nothing has run on Windows in CI yet.

### Data history costs storage

Every pin holds bytes in its system until the commit that names it is
dropped and `gc` releases it. `--pin record` skips the native ref and forks
from the recorded state, at the price of retention-bound recoverability.
Most store writes can be previewed as
[plans](05-reclaiming-storage.qmd#preview-before-you-write-plans).

### A clone is untrusted input

Nothing committed may choose an executable, an endpoint, SQL, or where a
secret is read from. What the boundary does *not* cover: a manifest's
locator still names the store tether reads and writes, so a hostile clone
can point an object at a bucket you can reach. Review manifests as you
would review code ([Security model](08-configuration.qmd#security-model)).

## Per backend

### Neon

Experimental: tested against a fake of the Neon API, not a live project.
This section is the one home for Neon's caveats.

**Lineage.** Pins are child branches, so a working branch cannot be deleted
while its pins exist. `gc --prune-bookmarks` plans it as `keep-branch:
cannot be deleted` and names the pins, even under `--force-prune`. `gc`
only drops leaf pins. `new` onto a *different* pin forks a sibling
(`<name>.2`, `.3`, ...) rather than reset a branch with children, while
`commit` then `new` reuses the branch, since it sits at the pin. Neon cannot
merge or promote a child into `main`: run production writes on the trunk
bookmark.

**A branch per commit.** Each commit that changes a Neon object adds a
branch. Neon plans cap branches per project (10 on Free) or bill those past
the allowance. `gc` releases pins no commit references, and `--pin record`
takes none at all. Pins are unprotected unless `protected_pins = true` in
`secrets.toml`. Neon will not delete a protected branch, and only paid plans
have a few, one per pinning commit. Branches *are* the storage
(`BRANCH_IS_STORAGE`): `gc --prune-bookmarks` never deletes a Neon working
branch holding unpinned data without `--force-prune`.

**Control plane.** Answers of 423 (another operation is running), 429 and
503 are retried with backoff for about a minute. `commit` refuses while
`pg_stat_activity` shows active writers, unless `--force`. Objects that
fingerprint one branch at once share one endpoint, created once.

**Fingerprint cost.** The LSN moves without user writes, so it is a
volatile address key. Only `commit_xid`, the newest committed transaction
id, and the lineage count as change; ids a restarted compute skipped never
commit, so they do not count. A snapshot may wake a suspended compute, and
creates the read-write endpoint on a branch with none. A plain `status`
does not fingerprint.

**Content is `{commit_xid, lineage}`.** `branch` in a Neon state is the
*lineage*: the object's source branch, when the branch read descends from
it. So a fork with no writes compares equal to the pin it was cut from. The
price: two sibling branches of one lineage whose newest commits share a
transaction id compare equal too. Neon exposes no content hash or history
query to tell them apart, which is why `gc` never judges a Neon branch by
its state alone, and `promote` is not offered.

### Files on unversioned storage

Observed: detectably but not recoverably drifted. `--file versioned` on a
versioned bucket makes a single remote object Addressable; local paths and
prefixes stay Observed. A local path's identity is its resolved form, so
re-pointing a symlink makes a new store: its pins stay safe, but its old
listings are not found.

### Iceberg catalog variance

S3 Tables disables maintenance when user refs exist. Use `--pin record`
there, so forks come from the snapshot id, valid until snapshot expiry.

### Delta has no refs

Versions are recorded, not pinned. `VACUUM` (7-day default) and log
retention (30 days) bound how long `open -r` works. A recreated table (new
metadata id) verifies as drifted, not re-addressed.

### Lance versions are branch-scoped

A branch deleted and created again restarts its version numbers, so a state
from its earlier life verifies as missing rather than opening the new one.
A pinned working branch outlives its bookmark until `gc` drops the tag,
since Lance refuses to delete a branch a tag references; `gc` reports it as
a failed `delete-branch`. A conditional fork onto an existing branch
compares, then deletes and creates it again, so a peer's branch created in
that window can be replaced.

### DuckLake attachments

A DuckDB-file metadata catalog can be attached only once per process. So
tether attaches per operation, and a `DuckLakeHandle` owns its attachment:
`close()` it (or use it as a context manager) before the next `status`, and
do not hold your own writer connection open in the same process. Postgres,
SQLite and MySQL catalogs have no such limit. Snapshots are catalog-wide,
and `table` only scopes the handle. Put `CREATE SECRET` statements in
`[backends.ducklake] init_sql` rather than credentials in the locator.

### Dolt working sets

Uncommitted changes on a branch are in no commit: a dirty branch is
reported and refused at `commit`. Credentials come only from the server's
`[uris."mysql://host:port"]` entry in `.tether/secrets.toml`, and a server
with none gets none. Dirty detection needs a Dolt with the `dirty` column
on `dolt_branches`; older servers report clean.

### git remotes

With `remote` set, a pin is a pin only once the tag push succeeds: a failed
push fails the `pin` and removes the local tag, and `unpin` deletes on the
remote first. A committed `remote` must name a configured remote; a URL
goes in `.tether/secrets.toml` as `[objects."<key>"] remote`.

## Performance

tether is an orchestrator: its cost is the network round trips it fans out,
not Python.

### Fan-out uses threads, not asyncio

Every backend SDK tether wraps (obstore, psycopg, pyiceberg, deltalake,
lance, duckdb, pymysql, `git`) is synchronous, and the per-object Python
work is microseconds. A thread pool gives the same wall-clock concurrency
without forcing an async protocol on backend authors. `snapshot`, `verify`
and the fork step of `new` all run concurrently. Credentials for one
profile or role are resolved once, however many threads ask.

### History walks are batched

`gc`, `verify --all-history`, `repair --all-history` and `upgrade` stream
every manifest at every commit through one `git cat-file --batch` process
(jj repositories are git-backed). Trees and blobs are cached by object id,
and each distinct `(system, state, pin)` is verified once. On a repository
with 200 commits and 5 objects this takes ~20-40 ms, against 6-12 s with one
process per read. History *rewrites* (`upgrade`, `abandon`) read and
transform only the commits that touch the dataset directory.

### Opens and refreshes pay for what changed

Every `open` re-reads the workspace and the manifests, but a file whose
size, mtime, ctime and inode are unchanged costs a `stat`, not a parse. A
changed `workspace.toml` also costs one VCS call, to check it is still
untracked.

### Fingerprints are metadata-only, except the first local one

A remote object is one `HEAD`, a prefix one paged `LIST`, and the etag is
the store's content hash. Local files are sha256-hashed, so timestamps do
not count as change. The hash is cached under `.tether/cache/` by
`(size, mtime_ns, ctime_ns, inode)`; ctime, because an overwrite that
restores the mtime cannot restore it. A file changed within two seconds of
the last read is read again. The first fingerprint of a tree reads every
byte (~1.5-3 GB/s per core, eight files at a time); every later one is an
`os.scandir` walk (~4-20 us per file) plus the files whose stat changed.

### Content diffs are metadata-only too

Each backend reads manifests, logs or catalog tables, never data. So
`diff --content` costs about one fingerprint per changed object: two
manifest reads for Icechunk and Lance, one log walk for Delta, one catalog
query for DuckLake, one prolly-tree diff for Dolt. Two stored file listings
diff in pure Python at ~50 ms per 100k paths.
